tamil-eelam.story:
Tamil Eelam is the name of an independent state that many Sri Lankan Tamils and their diaspora have sought in the north and east of Sri Lanka, an area of 18,880 square kilometres. In 1976 the Tamil United Liberation Front, a political party, adopted the Vaddukoddai Resolution calling for a free and sovereign state. In the 1977 election, on that promise, it won all 14 seats in the Northern Province and 4 of 10 in the Eastern Province. Sri Lanka's Sixth Amendment of 1983 then banned advocating a separate state.
The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), an armed group, went on to hold territory and run it much like a government. In those areas it had land, naval and air forces, local and higher courts, a civil police force, health and education boards, the Bank of Tamil Eelam, and radio and television stations. Kilinochchi was its administrative headquarters. The US State Department alleged that its judges had little training. In October 2003 the LTTE proposed an interim self-governing authority, which asked for regional autonomy in place of independence.
Government troops took Kilinochchi on 2 January 2009 and the last LTTE-held land on 18 May 2009. Almost all of the LTTE's leadership was killed, and thousands of its fighters surrendered. In March 2010 the Tamil National Alliance, the main Tamil party, dropped the demand for independence in favour of federalism, a system in which a region keeps its own powers inside the country.
In May 2010 a New York lawyer, Visvanathan Rudrakumaran, formed the Transnational Government of Tamil Eelam among Tamils abroad. Diaspora votes on independence were held in ten countries in 2009 and 2010, including Norway, France and Canada. No state has recognised Tamil Eelam or this body, and the Sri Lankan government has called it a ploy to perpetuate terrorism.

chechen-republic-of-ichkeria.story:
The Chechen Republic of Ichkeria was a state that governed most of the former Checheno-Ingush region of the North Caucasus from 1991 to 2000, on about 15,300 square kilometres, with Grozny as its capital. Russia regarded the territory as its own throughout.
In June 1991 an All-National Congress of the Chechen People met in Grozny at the urging of Dzhokhar Dudayev, a Soviet air force general, as the Soviet Union was falling apart. Its armed squads seized the local KGB headquarters and the regional parliament in September. Dudayev was elected president on 27 October 1991 and declared independence on 1 November. A secular constitution followed in March 1992. He later dissolved parliament and ruled by decree, and accounts date this to either June 1992 or 1993.
Russian forces entered Chechnya on 11 December 1994. The First Chechen War ended after Russia's defeat in the battle for Grozny in August 1996. On 12 May 1997 presidents Yeltsin and Aslan Maskhadov signed a peace treaty in Moscow. Sharia courts, which apply Islamic law, were set up after the war, a sharia-based criminal code was adopted in 1996, and in February 1999 Maskhadov declared an Islamic republic, which parliament said he had no power to do.
The Second Chechen War began in August 1999 and Grozny fell on 6 February 2000. In June 2000 Akhmad Kadyrov took charge of a Russian-backed administration. Recognition was slight. The Taliban recognised Ichkeria in January 2000, and Maskhadov rejected that. Georgia's Zviad Gamsakhurdia, himself then a leader in exile, also recognised it. Estonia voted to do so but never completed the act.
Akhmed Zakayev founded a government in exile in November 2007 and is based in London. On 18 October 2022 Ukraine's parliament declared Ichkeria temporarily occupied by Russia, which falls short of full diplomatic recognition. Armed units under the exile government's name were formed in Ukraine that month. Analyst Mark Galeotti describes the exile government's influence as marginal, and rival factions dispute who speaks for it.

donetsk-peoples-republic.story:
The Donetsk People's Republic was declared on 7 April 2014 by separatists gathered in the regional government building in Donetsk, in eastern Ukraine. Ukrainian media reported that no city or district council sent representatives. On 11 May 2014 a referendum in the separatist-held parts of the region was held, and its organisers claimed 89 per cent in favour of self-rule on a turnout of nearly 75 per cent. No government officially recognised the result.
The republic set up a parliament of 100 deputies called the People's Council. The Russian ruble came into official use on 1 January 2015, and it issued its own passports from March 2016. From June 2019 Russia began handing out its own passports to residents, with 470,000 issued across the Donetsk and Luhansk areas by July 2021 according to the Russian official Dmitry Kozak.
Ukraine passed a law on special status for the area in September 2014, declared the republics terrorist organisations in January 2015, and in 2018 declared the territory occupied by Russia. On 12 February 2015 leaders of both republics signed the Minsk II peace agreement, a plan for a ceasefire, local elections and special status for the area. It was never carried out, and each side blamed the other. Ukraine's parliament did not ratify the constitutional changes the deal called for. Ukraine said pro-Russian forces broke the ceasefire thousands of times, and it set a full ceasefire and Ukrainian control of the border as conditions for elections. Russia denied that its military was involved, said it was not a party to the agreements, wanted elections held before Ukraine regained the border, and in 2022 blamed Ukraine for the collapse.
No UN member recognised the republic until Russia did on 21 February 2022, three days before its full invasion of Ukraine. Syria followed in June and North Korea in July 2022. The republic's People's Council held a vote on joining Russia on 23 to 27 September 2022. Russia treated the vote as the basis for joining, and commentators widely called it a sham and various countries denounced it. Russia announced annexation on 30 September. On 12 October the UN General Assembly condemned it in Resolution ES-11/4, with 143 votes for, 35 abstentions and 5 against. Russia now treats the area as one of its federal regions, while Ukraine and most states still regard it as Ukrainian.

luhansk-peoples-republic.story:
The Luhansk People's Republic was declared on 27 April 2014 by pro-Russian activists gathered outside the regional government building in Luhansk, in eastern Ukraine. They seized the building two days later. A referendum on 11 May 2014 followed. Organisers said 96.2 per cent voted for self-rule on a turnout of 81 per cent, and no international observers were present.
From 2015 to early 2022 the republic held the land between the Russian border and the ceasefire line set by the Minsk agreements, the peace deals signed in 2014 and 2015. Its 2014 constitution did not spell out its borders. It had a 50-seat parliament, and in 2020 declared Russian its only state language. Pensions in 2015 were paid mostly in Russian rubles.
Russia recognised it on 21 February 2022, three days before invading Ukraine, and it said its recognition was based on the republic's constitutional claims to the entire Luhansk region. Syria and North Korea recognised it later that year. No UN member had done so before 2022. Officials reported 98 per cent in favour of joining Russia in a September 2022 vote, and Russia announced annexation on 30 September. The UN General Assembly condemned the annexation on 12 October by 143 votes to 5, with 35 abstentions. Russia treats it as one of its regions, and Ukraine and most other states regard it as Ukrainian territory. Freedom House, a US non-profit, scored the parts of Donbas held by the two republics 2 out of 100 for political rights and civil liberties in 2024.

bangladesh-1971.story:
Bangladesh broke away from Pakistan by war in 1971 and then gained general recognition. It had been East Pakistan, separated from West Pakistan by India. In the 1970 election the Awami League won 167 of East Pakistan's 169 seats, which gave it a majority of the 313 seats in Pakistan's National Assembly. The West Pakistani politician Zulfikar Ali Bhutto refused to let its leader, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, become prime minister.
On the night of 25 March 1971 the Pakistani army began Operation Searchlight, intended to take the main cities and end opposition within a month. Mujib was arrested. Independence was declared in Mujib's name on 26 March, and Major Ziaur Rahman read a declaration on his behalf over Chittagong radio. A provisional government was formed on 17 April 1971 in what is now Meherpur District, with Mujib as president in absence and Tajuddin Ahmad as prime minister. Bengali soldiers and civilians formed a guerrilla force called the Mukti Bahini.
India entered the war on 3 December 1971 after Pakistani air strikes. Bhutan was the first state to recognise Bangladesh, on 6 December. On 16 December Lieutenant General A. A. K. Niazi signed the surrender, and over 93,000 Pakistani troops gave themselves up. Estimates of the people killed by Pakistani forces and their allies range widely, from about 300,000 to 3,000,000 in Bangladeshi and reference sources, and independent researchers including The BMJ estimate 125,000 to 505,000 deaths.
Most UN members recognised Bangladesh during 1972, including the Soviet Union in January and the United States in April. China vetoed its UN application in 1972, citing unresolved questions over Pakistani prisoners, and recognised it on 31 August 1975.

republika-srpska.story:
Republika Srpska is one of the two parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it began as a breakaway Serb state. As Yugoslavia broke up, Bosnia's Serb politicians held a vote in Serb areas in November 1991, with 96 per cent support for staying in a federation with Serbia and Montenegro. On 9 January 1992 their assembly proclaimed a Republic of the Serb People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it took the name Republika Srpska on 12 August 1992.
The rest of Bosnia voted for independence in a referendum on 29 February and 1 March 1992, which most Serbs boycotted. The European Community and the United States recognised Bosnia in April 1992. The Bosnian War lasted until autumn 1995. In July 1995 more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed in and around Srebrenica, which the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal and the International Court of Justice later designated an act of genocide.
The Dayton Agreement, reached on 21 November 1995 and signed in Paris on 14 December, ended the war. Under it, Republika Srpska became one of Bosnia and Herzegovina's two entities, meaning self-governing halves of one state. It covers 48 per cent of the land and has about 35 per cent of the people. It has its own parliament, president and government, and it uses Bosnia's convertible mark. Sarajevo is its constitutional capital and Banja Luka its working one.
Conflicts with the Bosnian state continue. In 2015 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina ruled the 9 January holiday unconstitutional. In February 2025 the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina sentenced its president, Milorad Dodik, to one year in prison and a six-year ban from office for not complying with decisions of the international High Representative. The sentence was confirmed in August 2025, ending his term, and Dodik called it political persecution. Siniša Karan now holds the presidency.

republic-of-serbian-krajina.mechanism: Referendums limited to one ethnic group gave the republic a claim, but other states recognised Croatia within its old borders, and that left the republic with no international backing when Croatia took the land back.

free-aceh-movement.story:
The Free Aceh Movement, known as GAM, was an armed group seeking independence for Aceh, at the northern tip of Sumatra in Indonesia. Hasan di Tiro founded it in December 1976. Its first attack, in 1977, killed an American engineer working for Mobil. By 1979 government units had largely crushed it and di Tiro fled, and its leaders lived in exile in Stockholm for most of the 1980s and 1990s.
Fighting returned in waves. Indonesia declared Aceh a special military operations area in 1989. Total deaths across the whole conflict are estimated at over 15,000. An offensive in 2003 and 2004 reportedly cost GAM about half its members.
On 26 December 2004 a tsunami struck Aceh, and two days later GAM declared a ceasefire so that aid could get in. Talks in Finland began in February 2005, led by the former Finnish president Martti Ahtisaari. The agreement signed in Helsinki on 15 August 2005 ended the war. GAM disarmed, Indonesia withdrew the troops and police it had brought in from outside the region, about 500 exiled members were given amnesty and about 1,400 prisoners freed. Aceh gained local political parties and kept 70 per cent of income from local natural resources. A joint EU and ASEAN mission monitored it.
GAM disbanded its military wing in December 2005. Di Tiro returned to Indonesia in 2008. Former GAM figures went on to win the governorship in 2006 and 2012.

republic-of-west-papua.story:
West Papua is the western half of the island of New Guinea. The Dutch held it after Indonesia became independent and were preparing it for self-rule, with elections and a New Guinea Council in 1961. Indonesia also claimed it. The New York Agreement of 1962, signed by the Netherlands and Indonesia and approved by the UN General Assembly, passed it to Indonesia and promised a vote on its future after seven years.
That vote, the Act of Free Choice, was held from 14 July to 2 August 1969. In place of a poll of all adults, the Indonesian military selected 1,025 Papuans, and they reached a consensus for joining Indonesia. The UN's representative had asked for one person, one vote, and Indonesia refused, saying the 1962 agreement did not require it. The UN General Assembly took note of the result in Resolution 2504 without saying whether the vote met the agreement. Indonesia holds that this validates the act. Critics call it the Act of No Choice and say that voters were coached and threatened, and independence groups seek a new vote.
The Free Papua Movement began in December 1963. On 1 July 1971 two of its leaders, Seth Roemkorem and Jacob Prai, declared a Republic of West Papua and drafted a constitution. They soon fell out. The movement has armed units with no single commander, groups inside the territory that hold demonstrations, and leaders abroad who seek international support. Its peak of outside backing was an embassy that Senegal allowed in Dakar. No state recognises the republic.
Indonesia has labelled the movement a terrorist and separatist organisation since 2021. Fighting continues. Separatists held a New Zealand pilot from February 2023 to September 2024. On 11 February 2026 a pilot and co-pilot were shot dead as their plane landed, and a spokesperson for the movement's armed wing said the airline often carried Indonesian security forces. No political settlement exists.

quebec-referendums.story:
Quebec is a mainly French-speaking province of Canada. René Lévesque founded a movement for sovereignty-association in 1967, meaning independence combined with an economic partnership with Canada, and in 1968 it merged into the Parti Québécois. The party won provincial power in 1976.
Its first referendum, in 1980, concerned sovereignty-association and was rejected by 60 per cent to 40 per cent. The party returned to power in 1994 under Jacques Parizeau and held a second referendum in 1995, in which negotiating a partnership with Canada was optional. No won by 50.6 per cent to 49.4 per cent, a margin of 54,288 votes out of more than 4.7 million. Parizeau blamed money and ethnic votes, was widely criticised, and resigned.
The Supreme Court of Canada was then asked whether Quebec could leave on its own. In its opinion of 20 August 1998, it said no under both Canadian and international law. Secession would need a constitutional amendment. International law gives a right of unilateral secession only to peoples under colonial rule or foreign occupation, and to those denied meaningful self-determination inside a state. It also said that a clear vote on a clear question would oblige the rest of Canada to negotiate.
Parliament followed with the Clarity Act, which lets the House of Commons decide whether a question is clear and requires a clear majority. Sovereignists widely reject it as illegitimate. In May 2026 a Léger poll found 32 per cent for independence and 68 per cent against. The Parti Québécois won the provincial election of 5 October 2026 without a majority. Its leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, has said he will hold another referendum but not while Donald Trump is US president, which rules out a vote before 2029.

add_sources.t: Separatists win Quebec election but fall short of majority

ambazonia.story:
Ambazonia is the name separatists use for the English-speaking Northwest and Southwest Regions of Cameroon. After the First World War, German Kamerun was split into French and British mandates. In a UN plebiscite on 11 February 1961, voters in British Southern Cameroons could choose union with Nigeria or with Cameroon, with independence not on the ballot, and about 70 per cent chose Cameroon. It federated as West Cameroon on 1 October 1961. A referendum in 1972 replaced the federation with a single unitary state, ending its autonomy.
The lawyer Fongum Gorji Dinka coined the name in the 1980s and announced a Republic of Ambazonia in a 1985 memorandum, for which he was jailed. Other activists made declarations in 1999 and 2006. In November 2016 English-speaking lawyers, students and teachers began strikes and protests. The government cut phone and internet connections in early 2017.
On 1 October 2017 a separatist coalition unilaterally declared independence. At least 17 people were killed in protests afterward. Late in 2017 Cameroon sent a large military force to the regions, and a guerrilla war began. Cameroon's government said the declaration had no legal weight. On 5 January 2018 the Interim Government, including its president Sisiku Ayuk Tabe, was arrested in Abuja, Nigeria, and sent to Cameroon, and in 2019 a Cameroonian court gave Ayuk Tabe and followers life sentences on terrorism charges. Rival leaders inside the movement then disputed who governs.
As of 2023 government forces largely held the towns and separatist militias many remote rural areas. Many militias have enforced a school strike since 2017. Reported abuses by separatists include kidnappings and the killing of civilians suspected of collaboration, and reported abuses by government forces include burning villages, enforced disappearances, executions without trial and torture. By early 2025 infighting and rebel attacks on civilians had increased. The UN Security Council held an informal meeting on the crisis in 2019. No country has recognised Ambazonia.

azawad.story:
Azawad is the name given to the northern part of Mali, covering about 60 per cent of the country's land, including the regions of Timbuktu, Kidal and Gao. It is thinly populated, with about 1.5 people per square kilometre. The National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad, known as MNLA, is a mainly Tuareg rebel group that began an uprising on 17 January 2012.
With the Islamist group Ansar Dine, the MNLA took Kidal and Gao in March 2012 and Timbuktu in April. On 6 April Bilal Ag Acherif signed a declaration of independence in Gao, with Timbuktu as the intended capital. The African Union said the declaration had no value. ECOWAS, the West African regional body, called it null and void and said it could use force. France and the United States also rejected it.
On 26 May the MNLA and Ansar Dine announced a pact to create an Islamist state, and the MNLA later withdrew. In June, MOJWA and Ansar Dine, both Islamist groups, drove the MNLA out of Gao and Timbuktu, and by 12 July Ansar Dine had overrun its last towns. On 14 February 2013 the MNLA renounced its claim to independence and asked Mali to negotiate. A peace deal, the Ouagadougou Agreements, followed in June 2013, though fighting resumed. A proposed 2017 referendum on autonomy was postponed. On 30 November 2024 four Azawad movements merged into the Azawad Liberation Front. In April 2026, in an offensive alongside the al-Qaeda-linked group JNIM, it captured Kidal, and it now holds parts of northern Mali, some of them jointly with JNIM. No state recognises it.

add_sources.t: Territory of the Azawad Liberation Front
JNIM and allied rebels surge across Mali

zanzibar.story:
Zanzibar is a group of islands off East Africa. The United Kingdom ended its protectorate on 10 December 1963 and Zanzibar became an independent constitutional monarchy under its Sultan. On 12 January 1964 a revolution overthrew Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah, who fled, and a People's Republic was formed, led by the Afro-Shirazi Party. Estimates of the dead range from several hundred to 20,000, and most were Arabs and Indians.
In April 1964, about three months later, the new republic merged with mainland Tanganyika, and the union was soon renamed the United Republic of Tanzania. So Zanzibar was a separate state for about four months.
Zanzibar still has its own government inside Tanzania, the Revolutionary Government of Zanzibar, with its own president, Revolutionary Council and House of Representatives of 81 members. Tanzanian Prime Minister Mizengo Pinda said in July 2008 that there is no such thing as Zanzibar's sovereignty in the Union Government unless the constitution is changed. On 31 July 2010, 66.2 per cent of voters approved a constitutional change to let rival parties form governments of national unity.

basque-independence.story:
The Basque Country lies on both sides of the western Spanish and French border. A political movement for a Basque nation began in the 1890s with Sabino Arana, and the Basque Nationalist Party was founded around him in 1895. During the Spanish Civil War, in October 1936, the Basque Country gained autonomy from the Spanish Republic and José Antonio Agirre became its president. Basque troops surrendered to Franco's Italian allies at Santoña in 1937, and leaders fled abroad, with the exiled government settling in New York during the Second World War.
Students frustrated with that party's moderate position founded ETA on 31 July 1959. Its non-negotiable demand was an independent state across northern Spain and southern France. Between 1968 and 2010 it killed 829 people, including 340 civilians. After Spain returned to democracy in 1978 Basque autonomy was restored, and the Basque Nationalist Party has led the autonomous region for most of the time since the early 1980s. ETA announced a definitive end to armed activity in October 2011, gave up its weapons in April 2017 and said it had dissolved in 2018.
The main legal attempt was the Ibarretxe Plan, named for regional president Juan José Ibarretxe. It proposed free association with Spain on equal terms, with a right to self-determination. The Basque Parliament approved it on 30 December 2004 by 39 votes to 35. On 1 February 2005 the Spanish Congress refused even to debate it, by 313 votes to 29 with 2 abstentions. In 2026 a Basque government poll found 24 per cent support for independence and 37 per cent against.

kashmir-self-determination.story:
Kashmir was a princely state, a territory with its own ruler under British supremacy in India. When Britain left in 1947 its Maharaja, Hari Singh, faced an advance by Pakistani tribesmen and soldiers. On 26 October 1947 he signed an instrument of accession to India, and Indian troops were flown in the next day. India called the accession provisional, subject to a reference to the people, and treats it as the legal basis of its claim. Pakistan argued that the Maharaja no longer had authority to accede, since his people had revolted and he had fled his capital. Two days earlier, rebels had formed a provisional Azad, or Free, Kashmir government at Palandri.
On 21 April 1948 UN Security Council Resolution 47 called for a ceasefire, withdrawal of Pakistani fighters, a reduction of Indian forces, and then a plebiscite, a vote of all the people, on accession. The ceasefire took effect on 1 January 1949. No withdrawal happened and no plebiscite was held. India withdrew its offer of one in 1954. Today India holds about 55 per cent of the land and 70 per cent of the people, Pakistan about 30 per cent including Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, and China about 15 per cent including Aksai Chin.
In 1989 an insurgency began in the Kashmir Valley, led at first by the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front, which sought an independent state. Groups that favoured merger with Pakistan later came to the fore. India accuses Pakistan of arming and training militants. Pakistan officially says it gives only moral and diplomatic support, though its former president Pervez Musharraf said in 2015 that the state had supported and trained insurgent groups in the 1990s. By the end of the 1990s more than 30,000 people had died in estimates by historians, and upward of 100,000 Kashmiri Hindus had left in the early 1990s.
Article 370 of India's constitution had given the Indian-held state its own constitution, flag and internal autonomy. On 5 August 2019 a presidential order ended this, and parliament split the state into two union territories, directly under national government, from 31 October 2019. Phone and internet lines were cut and political leaders detained. On 11 December 2023 India's Supreme Court upheld the change unanimously, called Article 370 temporary, and told the government to restore statehood as soon as possible.

set.stopped_by: Indian government; the plebiscite was never held

darfur-self-determination.story:
Darfur is the western region of Sudan. In February 2003 rebels of the Sudan Liberation Movement and the Justice and Equality Movement (JEM) began attacking government positions, accusing the government of oppressing the non-Arab population. Armed militias known as the Janjaweed fought the rebels. The government publicly denied supporting them, while evidence indicates it gave them money and weapons and coordinated joint attacks. Estimates of the dead vary. A research centre, CRED, estimated 178,258 to 461,520 excess deaths in January 2010. The UN Security Council referred the situation to the International Criminal Court in 2005, and in 2025 that court convicted the Janjaweed leader Ali Kushayb of war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The rebels asked mostly for autonomy. JEM said in September 2007 that it would move from demanding self-determination to independence if talks failed. A 2006 peace deal included a referendum on the region's status. A 2011 deal signed at Doha replaced it, and a Darfur Regional Authority was created. A deal signed at Juba on 31 August 2020 gave signatory groups seats in the national government.
After war broke out between Sudan's army and a paramilitary force called the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the RSF and its allies drafted a founding charter at a conference in Nairobi in February 2025. A transitional framework followed on 4 March and the RSF's commander, Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, announced a Government of Peace and Unity on 15 April 2025. Its presidential council and cabinet were named on 26 July 2025. It claims all of Sudan, is based in the Darfur city of Nyala, and says it has a 15-member presidential council and a two-chamber legislature.
By November 2025 it controlled all of Central, East, South and West Darfur, most of North Darfur and West Kordofan. A Future Bank opened in Nyala in January 2026, and a parallel central bank and new banknotes followed in May 2026. Sudan's government calls it fictitious. The African Union told members not to recognise it. Several states, including the UK, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Pakistan, objected to it, and no state has recognised it.

republic-of-ararat.mechanism: A small armed body held a mountain area and declared a state, with an appeal to the League of Nations as its only legal step. It received no outside backing, and Turkey retook the land.

western-australia-1933.story:
Western Australia voted in 1900 to join the new Australian federation. Campaigns to leave began early, and motions were moved in the state parliament in 1902, 1904 and 1906. In the 1920s and 1930s the Secession League and the Dominion League campaigned for it.
On 8 April 1933, on the same day as a state election, 68 per cent of 237,198 voters supported leaving Australia. The governing party lost the election, but the new Labor government sent a delegation to London to ask the British Parliament to act, because Australia's constitution had been passed as a British law. A select committee of the British Parliament met for about 18 months and refused to consider the request, stating that it could not legally grant secession. The Secession League had disappeared by 1938.
Small movements came back later. The mining businessman Lang Hancock founded a Westralian Secession Movement in 1974, and a WAxit party formed in 2016. In an October 2020 poll, 28 per cent of Western Australians supported leaving.

set.stopped_by: Select committee of the UK Parliament

national-unity-government-myanmar.story:
On 1 February 2021 the army of Myanmar seized power after the National League for Democracy had won the 2020 general election. Members elected in that vote formed a committee called the CRPH and said it was the country's lawful parliament. On 16 April 2021 the CRPH named the National Unity Government, including members of other parties and independents, with Duwa Lashi La as acting president and Mahn Win Khaing Than as prime minister. Aung San Suu Kyi and Win Myint were named to posts but were in custody.
It announced an armed wing, the People's Defense Force, on 5 May 2021, and launched a declared defensive war on 7 September 2021. The junta's State Administration Council declared the NUG illegal and a terrorist organisation. In September 2022 the NUG said that the junta had lost control of half the country, a figure that is its own claim. In January 2025 it said it would base its headquarters in Sagaing Region, inside Myanmar. Its cabinet members are in hiding within the country. The military held elections in December 2025 and January 2026, which critics and Western governments called a sham, and on 3 April 2026 a parliament dominated by its allies and appointees elected the army chief, Min Aung Hlaing, president.
Recognition has come from parliaments and not from states. The European Parliament adopted a resolution in October 2021 recognising the CRPH and NUG as legitimate representatives. The Inter-Parliamentary Union treats the CRPH as a legitimate partner in dialogue. No UN member state has formally recognised the NUG. A 2021 deal that involved China and the United States kept Kyaw Moe Tun, appointed in 2020, in Myanmar's UN seat, and the UN rejected the NUG's attempts to replace him. It has offices in the US, the UK, Norway, France, the Czech Republic, Australia and South Korea, which are not recognised diplomatic missions.
The NUG reported raising US$42 million by May 2022, mostly spent on weapons and on supporting striking civil servants. Sales of property brought more: about $10 million for a Yangon home linked to the army chief, about $9.3 million for seized land in Mandalay, and about $10 million in 18 hours from pre-sales of flats on military-owned land. It also sold gem mining rights and issued bonds. In March 2026 it and four ethnic armed groups founded a joint council for a federal democratic union.

add_sources.t: Myanmar junta chief Min Aung Hlaing elected president

east-turkestan.story:
East Turkestan is the name that independence movements, chiefly among the Uyghur people, use for the region China calls Xinjiang. A first East Turkestan Republic formed in 1933 after a rebellion in Kashgar against the Republic of China, and a Hui-led army division put it down in 1934.
A second republic held three northern districts, Ili, Tarbaghatai and Altai, from 1944 to 1949 with secret Soviet help. After the Chinese Civil War, the People's Liberation Army took over Xinjiang in 1949, and that republic ended.
An East Turkistan Government in Exile was founded in Washington, D.C., on 14 September 2004. China treats all support for independence as terrorism, extremism and separatism, and supporters face harsh criminal penalties. In 2005 the author Nurmemet Yasin was given ten years in prison for inciting separatism. Most states and international organisations do not use the name officially.

navajo-nation.story:
The Navajo Nation is a Native American government in the United States, with land of about 27,400 square miles across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah. Its reservation was set up by treaty in 1868, approved by the United States the same year, and it reached its present borders in 1934. Federal law treats it as a government within the United States and not as a foreign state.
It has its own three-branch government, set up by a 1989 reform. Its 24-member Council passes laws, an elected president runs the executive, and its courts have a Supreme Court, created under that name in 1985, with ten judicial districts as of 2010. About 180 tribal police officers served in 2023. Its voters rejected a proposed written constitution, and its 110 local chapters gained powers under a 1998 act.
Its powers have real effects and clear limits. In March 2020 it imposed stay-at-home orders and curfews across the reservation during COVID-19. US courts can narrow those powers. In Arizona v. Navajo Nation, on 22 June 2023, the US Supreme Court ruled that the federal government has no obligation to secure water for the tribe, although the 1868 treaty reserved water for the reservation.

set.challenge: US Supreme Court ruled in 2023 that the US has no duty to secure its water

greenland-home-rule.story:
Greenland was a Danish colony until the Danish constitution of 1953 made it a county of Denmark and gave its people Danish citizenship. After a referendum on 17 January 1979 a Home Rule Act took effect on 1 May 1979. Greenland's parliament gained control of some internal policies, while Denmark kept foreign policy, security and natural resources. Greenland left the European Economic Community in 1985, while Denmark stayed in.
On 25 November 2008, 76.22 per cent of voters backed more self-government. The Self-Government Act of 21 June 2009 added 33 areas that Greenland may take over, including courts, police and natural resources. Denmark keeps citizenship, monetary policy, security, foreign affairs and defence. Greenland has its own offices in Brussels and Washington.
The Act recognises Greenlanders as a separate people under international law. Section 21 sets out a legal route by which Greenland's government can begin a move to independence. Money is the practical limit. Denmark's annual grant was 4.3 billion kroner in 2024, and Danish aid made up over 20 per cent of Greenland's economy from 2019 to 2023. Since 2025 the United States under President Donald Trump has threatened to annex Greenland.

manchukuo.story:
Manchukuo was a state set up in north-eastern China under Japanese control. Japan invaded Manchuria after the Mukden incident of 18 September 1931. A council of local figures proclaimed Manchukuo on 18 February 1932 and it was formally established at Hsinking on 1 March, with Puyi, the last emperor of China, as Chief Executive. Japan formally recognised it on 15 September 1932. In 1934 it became a monarchy with Puyi as emperor.
It had its own banknotes and banks, and it bought the Chinese Eastern Railway from the Soviet Union in 1935. It received limited recognition, mainly from states aligned with the Axis. An inquiry for the League of Nations, the Lytton Report of October 1932, found that Manchukuo could not have been formed without Japanese troops and was not a genuine independence movement. The League's assembly adopted the report, and Japan gave notice in March 1933 that it would leave the League.
The Soviet Union declared war on Japan and invaded on 8 August 1945. After Japan's surrender, Puyi abdicated on 17 August and the state was dissolved.

set.challenge: The League of Nations adopted the Lytton Report, which refused to recognise Manchukuo

islamic-state-2014.story:
The Islamic State is an armed group that seized large parts of Syria and Iraq. On 29 June 2014 it declared a worldwide caliphate, a state claimed to be the rightful rule over all Muslims, and named Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi as its caliph. Raqqa in Syria was its de facto capital. It reached its largest area in May 2015, and it ruled about 12 million people by the end of that year, on a budget above US$1 billion.
It behaved like a government in some ways. It taxed people, sold oil and ran councils that handled legal matters, and it issued a penal code in 2015 with punishments including floggings, amputations and crucifixions. Its attempt at a gold dinar saw little use. It also carried out mass killings, including of Yazidis in Iraq, which have been recognised as genocide. The UN designated it a terrorist organisation, which subjects it to sanctions in every member state, and no government recognised it as a state.
Iraqi forces took Mosul on 20 July 2017, and the Syrian Democratic Forces took Raqqa that October. It lost its last Syrian territory at Al-Baghuz Fawqani in March 2019, and a US raid killed al-Baghdadi on 27 October 2019. Its remaining members operate as insurgent cells, and its African affiliates kept a significant territorial presence as of 2025.

hatay-state.story:
The Sanjak of Alexandretta was a district of the French Mandate of Syria, with a mix of Turks, Arabs, Alawites and Armenians. Turkey wanted it when the Mandate ended. Turkey's government coined the name Hatay and raised the issue at the League of Nations, and France, the UK, the Netherlands, Belgium and Turkey then drafted a constitution for the district, which took effect in November 1937.
On 2 September 1938 the assembly proclaimed the Hatay State, under joint French and Turkish military supervision. It had 40 members, 22 of them Turks. On 29 June 1939, after a referendum, the legislature voted to dissolve the state and join Turkey. Critics called the vote rigged, because Turkey reportedly brought in tens of thousands of Turks from outside to register and vote.
France reportedly encouraged the annexation, hoping to keep Turkey from allying with Germany. Syria's President Hashim al-Atassi resigned in protest. The last French officials left Antakya on 23 July 1939, and many Arabs and Armenians fled to Syria.

bangsamoro.story:
The Moro are Muslim peoples of the southern Philippines. Nur Misuari founded the Moro National Liberation Front on 21 October 1972, a month after martial law was declared. The Tripoli Agreement of 23 December 1976, brokered by Libya, promised autonomy, and an Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was created in 1989. A breakaway group, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, led by Salamat Hashim, kept fighting.
The government and that group signed a Comprehensive Agreement on 27 March 2014. President Duterte signed the Bangsamoro Organic Law on 26 July 2018, and voters approved it in January and February 2019. The new government was inaugurated on 29 March 2019, with the former rebel leader Murad Ebrahim as chief minister. Abdulraof Macacua later took the post.
The region has a Parliament mandated at 80 members, a chief minister and cabinet, Shari'ah courts for Muslims which non-Muslims may choose to use, and powers to levy its own taxes. The law states that it remains an inseparable part of the Philippines. On 9 September 2024 the Philippine Supreme Court mostly upheld the law but ruled that Sulu is not part of the region, because a simple majority of its voters opposed joining in 2019. The first election for the parliament, postponed several times, was held on 14 September 2026, and no party won a majority.

republic-of-crimea-2014.story:
Crimea is a peninsula on the Black Sea that was an autonomous republic of Ukraine. On 26 and 27 February 2014 armed men without insignia took over its parliament and government buildings. Russia at first denied involvement and called them local self-defence units, and President Putin later said they were Russian troops. While they occupied the building, on 27 February, the parliament voted to hold a referendum and dismissed the regional government. Ukraine's interim government declared the votes illegal.
On 11 March the Crimean parliament said it would declare independence and ask to join Russia if voters agreed. On 14 March Ukraine's Constitutional Court ruled the referendum unconstitutional. It was held on 16 March, with official results of about 95.5 per cent for joining Russia on 83 per cent turnout. A report by Evgeny Bobrov, a member of the Russian president's Human Rights Council, suggested these were inflated, estimating 50 to 60 per cent support and 30 to 50 per cent turnout.
On 17 March Crimea declared itself the independent Republic of Crimea, and President Putin recognised it as a sovereign state by decree the same day. On 18 March the treaty for its accession to Russia was signed. On 27 March the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 68/262, which is not binding, by 100 votes to 11 with 58 abstentions, calling the referendum and the change of status invalid. Russia defends the vote as self-determination and cites Kosovo as a precedent. Ukraine treats the peninsula as its own territory.

naga-independence.story:
The Nagas are peoples of the hills between India and Burma. In 1929 the Naga Club asked the British Simon Commission to let the Nagas choose their own future after the British left. A local council set up under British officials in 1945 was reorganised as the Naga National Council in February 1946.
Zapu Phizo sent a telegram to the UN and Delhi on 14 August 1947 announcing a free Naga nation, which was intercepted and never delivered, and he declared Nagaland independent the next day, the same day India became independent. On 16 May 1951 the Council held its own plebiscite and claimed that 99.9 per cent of Nagas wanted independence, a figure India and Assam rejected, and it is unclear who took part. On 22 March 1956 Phizo formed a Naga Central Government, renamed the Federal Government of Nagaland in 1959.
India made Nagaland one of its states in 1963. On 11 November 1975 a group of Naga delegates signed the Shillong Peace Accord with India. In 1980 a faction led by Isak, Muivah and S. S. Khaplang broke away to form the National Socialist Council of Nagaland. Ceasefire talks took place in the 1990s, and India's government reached a peace deal with insurgents in 2015.

khalistan.story:
Khalistan is the name of a proposed Sikh state in the Punjab region of India. Calls for it appeared in a 1940 pamphlet. In 1973 the Akali Dal, a Sikh party, adopted the Anandpur Sahib Resolution, which sought more state autonomy. Jagjit Singh Chohan, in the diaspora, set up a Council of Khalistan around 1979 and declared a Republic of Khalistan in 1980.
From 1 to 8 June 1984 the Indian army carried out Operation Blue Star to remove the Sikh preacher Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale and his armed followers from the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar. Army figures gave 83 soldiers dead and the government 493 militants and civilians. Rajiv Gandhi later acknowledged over 700 soldiers killed, and independent estimates put civilian deaths at over 5,000. Two of her Sikh bodyguards assassinated Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on 31 October 1984. In the anti-Sikh riots that followed, the government counted about 3,350 dead, and independent estimates run from about 8,000 to 17,000.
On 29 April 1986 an assembly of separatist Sikhs at the Akal Takht declared an independent Khalistan, and militant groups fought an insurgency that faded by the mid-1990s. Khalistan was a member of the Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization for part of 1993, and its membership was permanently suspended in 1995.
Since 2021 the group Sikhs for Justice has run an unofficial, non-binding referendum among Sikhs abroad, with votes in Australia, Canada, New Zealand, Italy, England and the United States. In India's 2024 general election two candidates described as pro-Khalistan won seats as independents.

confederate-states.story:
Between December 1860 and February 1861, seven southern US states declared they had left the Union, starting with South Carolina on 20 December. They acted to protect slavery after Abraham Lincoln's election, and four more states joined after the fighting began. Their delegates met at Montgomery, Alabama, and formed the Confederate States of America on 8 February 1861, with a constitution and the Confederate dollar. Its capital moved to Richmond, Virginia, that May.
The Civil War began on 12 April 1861, when Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour. No foreign government officially recognised the Confederacy, and neither did the United States. Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox Court House on 9 April 1865, and the Confederate government had dissolved by May.
The legal question was settled by the Supreme Court in Texas v. White on 12 April 1869. Chief Justice Chase wrote that the Constitution does not permit a state to leave on its own, and that Texas's act of secession was absolutely null. He said that there was no place for reversing the union except through revolution or through the consent of the states.

herzeg-bosnia.story:
Herzeg-Bosnia was a Croat quasi-state inside Bosnia and Herzegovina during the wars that followed the breakup of Yugoslavia. It was established on 18 November 1991 as the Croatian Community of Herzeg-Bosnia with Mate Boban as president. Mostar was its designated capital, though it was run from Grude. The Bosnian government declared it unlawful five days later, and the Constitutional Court ruled its proclamation unconstitutional on 14 September 1992. It declared itself a republic at Grude on 28 August 1993, which the Bosnian government did not recognise.
Fighting between Croats and Bosniaks grew through late 1992 and escalated in early 1993. The Washington Agreement of 18 March 1994 ended that war, and Herzeg-Bosnia was to be merged into the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On 14 August 1996 the sides agreed it would be formally abolished by the end of that month.
In 2013 the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia convicted six of its leaders of taking part in a joint criminal enterprise against the non-Croat population. The tribunal upheld guilty verdicts against the six in November 2017.

alaska-purchase.story:
The Alaska Purchase was the sale of Russia's colony in North America to the United States. William H. Seward, the US Secretary of State, and Eduard de Stoeckl, a Russian diplomat, signed the treaty at 4 in the morning on 30 March 1867 after an all-night session. The price was $7.2 million for 1,518,800 square kilometres, about 2 cents an acre. Other counts give about 1.7 million square kilometres.
Russia needed money after its defeat in the Crimean War. The colony was hard to defend, Russia feared that British forces from Canada could easily take it, and the sea otter population it relied on had nearly died out. The US Senate ratified the treaty on 9 April by 37 votes to 2.
The treaty took effect on 18 October 1867, when the Russian flag was lowered at Sitka and the American flag raised. Nearly all Russians left, and most returned home by 1869. Seward estimated about 60,000 inhabitants, of whom about 50,000 were Inuit or Alaska Natives living outside Russian control, so most people there had not been under Russian rule before the sale.
Alaska was run as a department, then a district and then a territory, and it became a state in 1959.

mexican-cession.story:
The Mexican Cession was the transfer of about 1.36 million square kilometres from Mexico to the United States by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed on 2 February 1848. It ended the Mexican-American War and covered present-day California, Nevada, Utah, most of Arizona and parts of New Mexico, Colorado and Wyoming, about 55 per cent of the territory Mexico claimed before the war, leaving Texas out of the count.
The treaty mixes a peace settlement with a sale. The United States paid $15 million in yearly instalments of $3 million and took over $3.25 million that Mexico owed to US citizens.
People living there had one year to choose between US and Mexican citizenship, and over 90 per cent chose US citizenship. The treaty protected existing property rights. The US Senate removed the article that would have guaranteed land grants made by Spain and Mexico. A later protocol confirmed those grants under Mexican law, the United States later ignored it, and disputes over them continued into the 21st century.

florida-cession-1819.story:
Under the Adams-Onís Treaty, signed in Washington on 22 February 1819, Spain gave East and West Florida to the United States. John Quincy Adams negotiated for the United States and the Spanish ambassador, Luis de Onís, for Spain. The treaty also drew a border running from the Gulf of Mexico to the Pacific.
The money did not go to Spain. The United States agreed to compensate its own citizens for losses they said Spain had caused, and a commission paid out about $5 million before it closed in 1824. This sum is usually counted as the price of about 200,000 square kilometres.
The US Senate approved the treaty unanimously two days after signing. Spain delayed until October 1820, the Senate voted again, and the treaty took effect on 22 February 1821.

saint-barthelemy-sale.story:
Saint Barthélemy is a Caribbean island of 21 square kilometres that passed between owners several times. The Order of Saint John, a Catholic knightly order, held it in the 1600s, and the French West India Company bought it in 1665 with the order's other Caribbean holdings.
In 1784 King Louis XVI of France traded the island to Sweden for trading privileges in Gothenburg. The Swedes named the town of Gustavia after their king, Gustav III, and made it a free port, one where goods paid no customs duties. The colony lasted nearly a century.
After a status referendum in 1877, Sweden sold the island back to France, and it returned on 16 March 1878. The price was 320,000 French francs. Today it is a French overseas collectivity, a territory with its own council that remains part of France. It separated from Guadeloupe in 2007 and left the European Union in 2012. The 2023 census counted 10,660 residents.

gwadar-transfer-1958.story:
Gwadar is a port town on the Arabian Sea. It was an overseas possession of the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman from 1783 to 1958, a link that began with a grant from the Khan of Kalat to Sultan bin Ahmad.
On 8 September 1958 Oman handed Gwadar to Pakistan. Prime Minister Feroz Khan Noon and his wife, Viqar-un-Nisa Noon, are credited with convincing the British government to allow the handover. Sources disagree on the money. One reference list gives a price of 5.5 billion Pakistani rupees and an area of 15,210 square kilometres. Another account gives no official price and mentions a contribution of about $3 million from Prince Karim Aga Khan IV.
Gwadar became part of Makran district and a district of its own in 1977. Construction of the first phase of Gwadar Port began in 2007 at a cost of $248 million, and in 2013 the state-owned China Overseas Port Holdings acquired the port.
gwadar-transfer-1958.mechanism: A state transferred an overseas possession by agreement for money, with a third state's consent. Later a Chinese state-owned company acquired the port, which gave it control of a business and left sovereignty with Pakistan.

elten-selfkant-return.story:
After the Second World War the Netherlands took small pieces of German land. On 23 April 1949 Dutch troops occupied about 69 square kilometres, with almost 10,000 inhabitants in all. The largest parts were the town of Elten on the Rhine, with 3,235 people, and Selfkant near Sittard, with 5,665.
West Germany began negotiating for their return in March 1957. A treaty signed in The Hague on 8 April 1960 had West Germany pay 280 million German marks for the return of Elten, Selfkant and the village of Suderwick. The payment was described as compensation. The land went back on 1 August 1963, except for a hill of about 3 square kilometres near Wyler that the Netherlands kept.
Before the border moved, traders stored coffee and butter in the towns about to change country. At midnight the goods were on the other side of the border without having paid import tax. The night is remembered as Butter Night.

baltic-sale-1721.story:
In 1721 the Treaty of Nystad ended the Great Northern War between Russia and Sweden. Sweden recognised Russian control of Estonia, Livonia and Ingria, and Russia paid Sweden 2 million silver riksdaler for territory in south-east Finland. The area was about 100,000 square kilometres in all.
A sale of territory is a deal in which one government gives up its right to rule a place in return for money, normally by treaty. Private landowners may keep their deeds, while courts, taxes and police change hands.
baltic-sale-1721.mechanism: A war ended with a treaty that moved the land and included a payment to the side giving it up, so the treaty is partly a peace settlement and partly a sale.

danish-gold-coast-sale-1850.story:
In 1850 the United Kingdom bought the Danish Gold Coast from Denmark for £10,000. The area was about 12,000 square kilometres.
A sale of territory is a deal in which one government gives up its right to rule a place in return for money, normally by treaty. Private landowners may keep their deeds, while courts, taxes and police change hands.

dutch-gold-coast-sale-1872.story:
In 1872 the United Kingdom bought the Dutch Gold Coast from the Netherlands for 46,939.62 guilders.
A sale of territory is a deal in which one government gives up its right to rule a place in return for money, normally by treaty. Private landowners may keep their deeds, while courts, taxes and police change hands.

caroline-islands-sale-1899.story:
In 1899 Germany bought the Caroline Islands from Spain for 25 million pesetas. The area was 1,160 square kilometres.
A sale of territory is a deal in which one government gives up its right to rule a place in return for money, normally by treaty. Private landowners may keep their deeds, while courts, taxes and police change hands.

kammerwald-sale-1961.story:
In 1961 West Germany bought an uninhabited area of the Kammerwald from Luxembourg for a sum given as 53,277,370 Deutsche Marks, though another reference gives 35 million. The area was about 5 square kilometres.
A sale of territory is a deal in which one government gives up its right to rule a place in return for money, normally by treaty. Private landowners may keep their deeds, while courts, taxes and police change hands.

set.cost: Given as 53,277,370 Deutsche Marks; another reference gives 35 million

neom.story:
Neom is a planned development of 26,500 square kilometres in north-west Saudi Arabia, announced by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on 24 October 2017. It is run by a company set up in 2019 and wholly owned by the Public Investment Fund, the Saudi state's investment fund. The first cost estimate was $1.6 trillion, and by 2025 the estimate had grown to over $8.8 trillion.
The crown prince said Neom would operate independently of the existing government framework, with its own tax and labour laws and an autonomous judicial system. The best-known part, The Line, was announced in January 2021 as a city 170 kilometres long and 500 metres high for 9 million people.
About 20,000 people were expected to be moved. In April 2020 Abdul Rahim al-Huwaiti, of the Howeitat people, said security forces were trying to evict him, and they then shot him dead. They said he opened fire on them. An activist from his tribe disputes that and says he owned no firearms. In October 2022 the Specialized Criminal Court sentenced three members of the Howeitat to death for resisting displacement.
By 2025 The Line had been substantially scaled down or suspended, no new contracts were reported that year, and contracts were cancelled in March 2026. An island resort, Sindalah, opened in October 2024 and remained closed to the general public in 2025.

eko-atlantic.story:
Eko Atlantic is a private city being built on land reclaimed from the Atlantic Ocean at Lagos, Nigeria. Reclamation means making new dry land by pouring sand into the sea. The developer is South Energyx Nigeria, a company of the Chagoury group. The city project dates from 2003. About 9 square kilometres are being reclaimed in front of Bar Beach, behind a long sea wall, at a reported cost of about $6 billion.
It is a partnership in which private investors pay, the Lagos State government is a partner and the federal government gives support. Plans say the city will have its own bureaucracy, be treated as a separate municipality and include an offshore banking zone, and that it will provide its own water, waste handling, security, transport and power.
At least 250,000 residents are planned. As of November 2020 only a few buildings were complete, the best known being the Eko Pearl Towers.
Nearby residents say the project has made erosion and ocean surges worse, and critics say the state failed to involve them. In August 2012 a surge swept 16 people into the ocean and killed several. An opposition party blamed the sand filling and called for the project to stop.

laser-558.story:
Laser 558 was a pop station on a ship, the MV Communicator, anchored in international waters off the Thames Estuary from May 1984. The ship was registered in Panama through a company called Deka Overseas. Its disc jockeys and managers were American, and it used a pair of 25 kilowatt transmitters on 558 kHz.
BBC research reportedly put its audience at about four million in the UK and a similar number on the continent. On 9 August 1985 the UK Department of Trade and Industry chartered a ship, the Dioptric Surveyor, to watch Laser and Radio Caroline, and it was replaced in November by the Gardline Tracker.
Laser went off the air in late 1985 as advertising ran short, and the ship was then impounded on behalf of creditors. It came back on 1 December 1986 as Laser Hot Hits under new owners and closed for good at Easter 1987.

mv-narrative.story:
MV Narrative is a planned ship on which people would buy apartments and live while it sails around the world every three years. The company behind it, Storylines, launched in 2018 and first meant to buy a used ship before switching to a new one. It ordered the ship from the Brodosplit yard in Croatia in 2022, with 547 residences priced from about $600,000 to over $9 million.
Its start date has moved repeatedly, from 2025 to 2026 to 2027. An industry report in February 2025 described no steel cut. In 2026 the company cut its staff and asked people with $10,000 deposits held outside its trust account to wait for their money until a restructuring is finished. It says it has access to a $500 million bank guarantee and is still working out how to turn that into cash, and that it is working with a second yard as a backup.
A residential ship does not create a new jurisdiction. An industry listing gives its flag as Panama, which would mean Panama's law applies on board and each port's law applies when it calls there. A home on board is a purchase from a company, and buyers carry that company's risk.

set.anchor: Brodosplit shipyard, Split, Croatia, which received the order in 2022.

set.founder: Bob Denard and mercenaries; documents and a French official pointed to backing from African leaders

maldives-1988-coup-attempt.story:
On 3 November 1988 a Maldivian businessman, Abdullah Luthufi, who ran a farm in Sri Lanka, tried to seize the Maldives. A Sri Lankan Tamil armed group, PLOTE, supplied 100 to 200 fighters, who arrived in the capital, Malé, by sea.
President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom appealed for help. India flew about 500 paratroopers from Agra to Malé's airport, and they arrived about nine hours after his appeal. They rescued Gayoom and restored his government within hours. Reported deaths were 19, most of them mercenaries.
Some attackers fled toward Sri Lanka on a hijacked freighter, the MV Progress Light, with hostages. Indian warships caught it and commandos boarded it. In July 1989 India returned the captives to the Maldives for trial. They were sentenced to death, and under Indian pressure Gayoom changed the sentences to life imprisonment. Luthufi was among those convicted, and under Maldivian law his life term came to 25 years, which he has completed.

add_sources.t: Maldivian coup mercenary leader completes 25-year prison sentence

operation-gideon-2020.story:
Operation Gideon was a failed sea raid on Venezuela in May 2020 run with a private security company. Silvercorp USA was founded in 2018 by Jordan Goudreau, a former US Army Green Beret. On 16 October 2019 Goudreau signed a General Services Agreement with J. J. Rendón and Sergio Vergara, associates of the opposition leader Juan Guaidó. It set a retainer of $1.5 million. Guaidó and his allies denied that he signed directly and said Rendón and Vergara signed for him, and he denied knowing about the raid. Goudreau produced a seven-page document that he says carries Guaidó's signature. An earlier plan pitched by Goudreau cost $212.9 million, to be repaid from future oil sales.
Goudreau said about 60 men took part, and they left Colombia's Guajira Peninsula in two boats on 2 May 2020. The first was sunk near Macuto on 3 May, and six Venezuelan dissidents were killed. Goudreau announced the raid in a video that day. The second was intercepted off Chuao after most of its men had been dropped along the shore.
Two former Green Berets, Airan Berry and Luke Denman, were captured, and on 6 August 2020 a Venezuelan court sentenced them to 20 years after they admitted the charges. Both were freed on 20 December 2023 in a prisoner exchange between the United States and Venezuela. Venezuela issued warrants for Goudreau, Rendón and Vergara. In June 2023 Cliver Alcalá, who had publicly taken responsibility for the plan, pleaded guilty in the United States to providing material support to a terrorist group and to illegal transfer of firearms, in a case whose narcotics charges were dropped. In 2024 US prosecutors charged Goudreau with weapons smuggling for shipping about 60 AR-15 rifles to training camps without an export licence. He has not been convicted, and in October 2025 a judge ordered his arrest after he missed a court hearing.
operation-gideon-2020.mechanism: A contract with opposition figures gave a private company no legal authority in Venezuela. Those who took part faced the criminal law of Venezuela and the United States.

set.challenge: Six killed; two Americans captured, sentenced to 20 years and freed in a 2023 prisoner exchange

add_sources.t: Judge orders arrest of ex-Green Beret tied to failed Venezuela raid
Foley Foundation on detainee releases in Venezuela

assassination-jovenel-moise.story:
On 7 July 2021, at about 1 in the morning, Haiti's president, Jovenel Moïse, was killed at his home in Port-au-Prince. The accused attackers were identified as 28 foreigners, 26 of them Colombians, of whom at least 21 were former soldiers, and two Haitian Americans. A Miami security company, CTU Security, owned by Antonio Intriago, hired a man to recruit the former soldiers, and its company card paid for 19 plane tickets from Bogotá to Santo Domingo.
Three Colombians were killed in a police shootout, and 18 Colombians and the two Haitian Americans were arrested soon after. Because part of the planning happened in the United States, US law applied. Several people pleaded guilty in Miami and received life sentences, including Rodolphe Jaar, Germán Rivera García and Joseph Vincent. On 8 May 2026 a Miami federal jury convicted Arcángel Pretel Ortiz, Antonio Intriago, Walter Veintemilla and James Solages of conspiring to assassinate him. The defence argued that they believed they were acting on a Haitian court order to remove him and not to kill him.
In Haiti, 51 people were charged in February 2024. Hearings were paused during the country's gang war and resumed in May 2025. An appeals court later overturned those indictments and ordered a new investigation, and several judges and prosecutors withdrew, some citing their safety.

panama-ship-register.story:
Every merchant ship is registered with a country and flies its flag. That country's law then applies on board in most matters, wherever the ship sails. Panama's register is run by the state and accepts ships owned by foreigners as well as locals. Registers of this kind are called open registers, and their flags are often called flags of convenience.
It began with Law 63 of 15 December 1917, which let a vessel receive the flag on request. The first ship recorded was the Belén Quezada. Law 8 of 12 January 1925 set out the procedures and formally created the merchant marine registry. Decree-Law 7 of 1998 created the Panama Maritime Authority, which now runs it through about 70 offices around the world.
Panama was the world's largest flag from 1993 until 2023, when Liberia passed it by gross tonnage, a measure of a fleet's size. Panama still had far more ships, 8,254 against 5,052. In June 2016 it had about 8,831 ships of about 235 million gross tons, and in 2017 its ships were about 18 per cent of the world fleet. Registration and related activity brought about $162 million to the treasury as of December 2015.

add_sources.t: Liberia takes world's largest ship registry crown
